newsitem.title: FRANCE: UNIONS EXPECT 10,000 FOR RENAULT PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: UNIONS EXPECT 10,000 FOR RENAULT PROTEST.

text.p: Trade unions expect 10,000 people to take part in a demonstration at Renault SA headquarters on Tuesday to protest the carmaker's plans to cut jobs in France and close a Belgian plant, union officials said on Monday.
The protest is scheduled for 1000 GMT, ahead of a meeting at 1300 GMT of Renault's European works council which chairman Louis Schweitzer is expected to attend.

"We're going to ask for two things at the meeting -- that Renault reconsider the closure of the Vilvoorde plant (in Belgium), and for the start of negotiations to reduce working hours to preserve jobs under the (French) Robien law," CFDT spokesman Emmanuel Couvreur told Reuters.

"The demonstration is expected to draw between 4,500 and 5,000 Belgians, about the same number in France, and 50 to 100 workers from Spain," Couvreur said. He said some Portuguese workers may also attend.

A spokesman for the Communist-led CGT, the biggest union at Renault, said around 10,000 people were expected in all. He said the Belgian contingent would include relatives of Renault employees and workers from firms supplying the Vilvoorde plant.

Renault said on February 27 that it would close the plant, which employs 3,100 people, by the end of July as part of a programme to reorganise and streamline its European car assembly operations. Last week it also announced plans to cut 2,764 jobs in France this year, up from 1,640 job cuts in 1996.
The company has drawn fire from unions and French and Belgian politicians who say they are appalled by the brutality of the measures and the short notice.

Unions have organised work stoppages, marches and protests since the measures were announced, but the company and unions give widely disparate accounts of the extent to which Renault's 138,000 employees have participated in the labour actions.

The company, which is expected to report a loss on its operations of more than two billion francs for 1996, says the job cuts and plant closure are necessary in the face of growing competition in the weak European car market.
Renault is the smallest and weakest of Europe's six mass car manufacturers.

The CFDT said in a statement on Monday that the measures "address neither the problem of its size nor that of the market. Through this financial strategy of cost reductions and job cuts, Renault is downsizing...which can only lead to progressive weakening, putting its very existence at risk."
The unions have also called on workers at Renault's plants to carry out strikes of one hour or longer on Tuesday to support the protest.
